pitch_detail.notes: Park Butte Trail 603 crosses Sulfur Creek early (a log or footbridge that can turn into a ford at peak melt), then climbs through meadow and forest switchbacks to Morovitz Meadow about 2 miles in. Leave the Park Butte trail there and bear left onto the Railroad Grade trail. Morovitz is the last dependable running water.

Follow the narrow crest of the lateral moraine with the Easton Glacier falling away on the right; the edge is loose and exposed in wind. Camps sit around 5,600 ft or at Sandy Camp, rock-walled tent pads near 5,900–6,000 ft where the trail ends. Expect to melt snow for water from here up.

Rope up at the glacier edge and climb roughly north toward Sherman Peak, keeping east (climber's right) of the main crevasse bands. Cracks grow larger and more frequent higher up, so expect end-runs and snow-bridge crossings that shift through the season. Leave camp in the small hours for firm bridges, and wand the track: the slope is broad and featureless in whiteout.

Around 9,400–9,700 ft the route reaches the rim of steaming Sherman Crater, where sulfur gas is obvious; do not linger or descend toward the vents. Below Sherman Peak the slope is swept by rockfall, so cross it quickly, then trend west across the saddle to the eastern foot of the Roman Wall. This is the usual regroup and refuel spot.

About 1,000 vertical ft of sustained snow, mostly 35–40° with portions near 45°, the steepest ground on the route. It turns icy in cold or late-season conditions, and a rock outcrop above sheds stones, so stay right of the rocky rib and move steadily. Many parties face in to downclimb it on the way back.

The angle eases onto a very broad, nearly flat summit plateau. The true summit, Grant Peak, is a small snow bump at the far east-northeast edge rising only about 80 ft above the rest of the plateau. In cloud the plateau is easy to wander on, so follow your wands and a compass bearing back to the top of the Roman Wall.

pitch_detail.notes: Heliotrope Ridge trail climbs about 2,800 ft through forest and meadow, crossing Grouse, Kulshan and Heliotrope creeks, to camps on and around the Hogsback moraine near 6,000 ft. The creeks swell with afternoon melt, so cross them early in the day.

Rope up and climb south then southeast toward the Black Buttes, weaving through crevasse zones; late in the season some cracks span the whole slope and leave a single snowbridge. Higher up the track swings east under Colfax Peak, where the icefall off Colfax threatens the route: cross beneath it without stopping. Gain about 3,000 ft to the saddle.

The broad ice saddle at about 9,000 ft sits between Colfax Peak and the summit cone; it is a common rest stop. From it, climb roughly 300 ft east up the exposed pumice ridge on a boot-beaten path, where the terrain turns noticeably steeper and the Deming side opens up on the right.

From the top of the pumice ridge, climb the steep snow slope to the right of the Roman Wall's rock, roughly 9,300 to 10,400 ft. In low-snow years or after a freeze it is hard ice that demands careful crampon work, and it is the most exposed ground on the route. Descending, most parties face in on the steepest part, especially in whiteout.

The slope relents onto a flat snowfield between the old crater and the true summit, about ten minutes of walking to the Grant Peak high point. The plateau is fully exposed to wind and loses all definition in cloud, so mark the top of the Roman Wall before heading across.

review.changed: 5 → 5 entries, same labels. Notes rewritten from thin phrases to directions, elevations (9,000 ft saddle, ~300 ft pumice ridge, Roman Wall ~9,300–10,400 ft) and hazards (Colfax icefall, single-bridge crevasses, ice on the Roman Wall).

pitch_detail.notes: From high camp below the glacier, rope up and cross the lower Boulder Glacier heading northwest to the toe of the Boulder–Park Cleaver, near 6,800 ft. A few crevasses and icefall bands lie on this crossing. Parties that instead climb the glacier's central section meet far more broken ground and unreliable, undercut bridges by midsummer.

Follow the cleaver, mostly on its north side, with a short rock scramble around 7,800 ft; this middle section is largely crevasse-free. Flat bivy sites along the rib (around 7,200–7,500 ft) allow a shorter summit day, and a flat spot near 8,800 ft is the place to study the upper mountain. Higher, the snow can be steep, icy and exposed to rockfall, with crevasses close below.

At the large rock buttress near 9,300 ft, head up toward its toe and traverse south toward Sherman Crater on moderate snow, weaving through crevasses; the pattern here dictates the line and is very broken by midsummer. The traverse passes beneath the buttress, so helmets and pace matter. From the crater side, finish up steep glacier between the vents and the summit plateau.

Alternative to the snow traverse: climb the rock buttress above 9,300 ft directly on 4th-class ground, or skirt its north edge on a short snow or ice slope, then angle onto Grant Peak. Cliffs drop steeply near the summit, and the whole face gets early sun, so start early to be off it before rockfall begins.

review.changed: 2 → 4 entries. Added the lower glacier crossing and the Boulder–Park Cleaver below the two existing finish options (kept with their labels and grades; they are alternatives, not sequential). The route faces east, which drives the early-start note.
sources_consulted: search-result summary of summitpost.org Boulder Glacier / Cleaver page (403 to direct fetch)
review.other_findings: Stored beta reverses the order ('follow the Boulder-Park Cleaver northwest onto the lower Boulder Glacier'): sources cross the lower glacier NW to the toe of the cleaver, then climb the cleaver. Stored approach is also muddled ('moraine to the Boulder/Park Glacier near 6,300 ft and a high camp around 5,500 ft'); sources put high camp at ~5,000–5,500 ft below the glacier and the cleaver toe near 6,800 ft. Name/grade: MP files the line as 'Boulder-Park Cleaver'.

pitch_detail.notes: North Fork Sauk Trail to Mackinaw Shelter, then a steep 2,000 ft of switchbacks to the PCT at White Pass. A climbers' path traverses north past the White Chuck Glacier basin to Glacier Gap (about 7,250–7,300 ft), where the White Chuck and Suiattle glaciers meet and there is ample camping. The Red Creek ford can be a real early-season obstacle.

From Glacier Gap climb the ridge north, first on its left side, then moving right beneath Glacier Gap Peak, and regain the crest around 8,400 ft. The rock is loose throughout, so keep parties close together. Where the cleaver steepens, most parties put on crampons and helmets and step off the dirt onto snow.

Traverse right (northeast) onto the upper Suiattle Glacier and continue below the cliffs of Disappointment Peak to the upper Cool Glacier near 9,200 ft. The stretch under the cliffs, around 8,600 ft, is an active rockfall zone: cross it fast and without stopping, particularly on the way down once the snow softens. Rope up for the glacier once past it.

Climb the Cool Glacier westward to the col above Disappointment Peak at about 9,600 ft, passing medium to large crevasses that open wider as summer goes on. Alternative that avoids the glaciers: scramble over Disappointment Peak (9,755 ft) on 4th-class loose rock and drop about 150 ft to the same col. Most parties unrope at the col.

From the col follow the ridge north-northwest on a steep volcanic dirt path or snow, bearing up and left until an obvious moderate slope leads straight north to the summit ridge for the last 200–300 ft. That final slope is often firm snow near 35°, so keep the axe out; the sandy ridge is loose underfoot and sheds rock onto parties below.

pitch_detail.notes: Traverse around the south side of Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers (about 8,000–8,200 ft), then climb the Kennedy Glacier to the 8,800 ft saddle with the Ermine Glacier where the ridge begins. The glacier's left half holds few crevasses; low down the till below Kennedy Peak is a crumbling mess of big boulders. The 8,800 ft saddle is the last sure bivy.

Climb the ridge from 8,800 ft toward 9,900 ft on a mix of decomposing pumice and steep snow, with sections of 45–50° that most parties protect with pickets. Staying on snow with crampons on is often easier than the sandy rock; keep left past the first gendarme. The crest is exposed, with dirty ice on one side and unstable rock on the other.

The twin eroded lava towers of the Rabbit Ears sit at the very top of the initial ridge and only look like ears once above them. Pass through the notch and downclimb about 150 ft of class 3 rock to a small saddle. The rock is very loose in warm, dry weather; cold, snowy conditions freeze it in place and make this section far more manageable.

From the saddle, cross snow or loose rock along the ridge to the foot of an alpine ice face and climb it for one to two pitches until it rounds off. Mostly around 50°, with a short step that has run 60° to near-vertical in some years; reported grades range AI1 to AI2. Bring screws and pickets, and a second tool eases the steep step.

Top out onto the crater rim, watching for cornices and hidden holes along its edge. Drop into the crater and climb its steep wall on the left, which may be hard ice low down with crevasses opening late in the season, then make an easy traverse to a gap on the right and a short climb to the summit.

wa_mount_adams_northwest_ridge.skip_reason: Route identity is ambiguous, so pitch beta cannot be matched safely. The row is named Northwest Ridge, but its stored table and overview describe a 5-pitch AI1–2 snow/ice line on the 'west face of the North Ridge' with FA Molenaar/Johnson/Ostro/Startzell 1960. The five equal 121 m pitches look like length_m (610) divided by 5, not a source. Sources describe the actual Northwest Ridge as an unroped snow-and-talus ridge from the Adams Glacier high camp: ~30° snow, ~40° above 10,000 ft, a rock outcrop near 10,500 ft bypassed on the North Face of NW Ridge side, finishing at the Pinnacle (~12,000 ft) and crossing the crater to 12,276 ft. The nearby North Face of NW Ridge is AI2–3, ~2,000 ft, FA Givler/LeBlond/McGowan 1967. No source was found for the 1960 party. A human should decide which route this row is before a breakdown is written. Sources: mountainproject.com/route/125742502, search summaries of summitpost.org/northwest-ridge/158220 and wildsnow.com Adams North Face of NW Ridge.

pitch_detail.notes: From High Camp near 6,900–7,100 ft, climb the moraine and snow gully to the toe of the Adams Glacier and rope up. The lower glacier is moderate walking that steepens around 8,500 ft. Hold toward the right (west) third of the glacier from the start: the eastern flank carries an active icefall that has dropped multiple large seracs in a single afternoon.

Between about 9,200 and 11,800 ft the glacier pours through a steep icefall of seracs and crevasses. Low in it, expect a series of ice steps around 45°, each about a rope length, mixing steep snow, crumbly ice and hard glacial ice; most parties belay or run protection on pickets and screws. The line changes year to year and through the season.

The steepest ground, typically a 45° ice slope of about two pitches around 9,500–10,200 ft, followed by large crevasses that can force long lateral traverses to find a crossing. Some years a bridgeless crack must be rappelled into and climbed out of. Reported grades run AI2 to AI3. Stay out from under the seracs and keep moving.

Pass the upper icefall on whichever side the crevasses allow, working left onto easier névé that leads to the false-summit plateau. From there it is a long, gentle traverse across the summit plateau to the true summit at 12,276 ft. Top out early; the icefall below gets more active as the day warms.

sources_consulted: search-result summaries of summitpost.org/adams-glacier/686134, the Mountaineers Adams Glacier trip report and the Santiam Alpine Club 2003 trip report (lower icefall of three ~45° ice steps, each about a pitch)

pitch_detail.notes: Ptarmigan Trail 216A climbs gently through open forest from the 3,700 ft trailhead to the Loowit Trail junction at timberline, about 4,800 ft. This is the last shade and the last water, and only small seasonal trickles at that; carry all water from the car. A climbing permit is required above 4,800 ft.

Above timberline, scramble up the blocky lava boulders of Monitor Ridge, following a line of large wooden posts to about 7,000 ft. The rock is coated in abrasive ash. In fog, losing the post line is the main route-finding hazard: a small drift puts you on steep, loose ground off-route, so do not move on until the next post is in sight.

A USGS GPS station near 7,000 ft marks where the posts end. The last roughly 1,300 ft to the rim is unmarked loose pumice, ash and scattered rock, like climbing a sand dune; the rock ribs are firmer than the ash gullies beside them. In spring this is a snow climb that calls for axe, crampons and avalanche awareness.

The rim first reached is not the high point; the true summit (8,363 ft) is about a quarter mile west along the rim with some scrambling. The rim carries overhanging cornices that have repeatedly collapsed into the crater, so stay well back from the edge and never step onto snow that overhangs it. Note where you arrived so you can find the route down.

review.changed: 3 → 4 entries. Added the rim traverse to the true summit with the cornice hazard; existing three labels kept, notes rewritten with the 4,800 ft junction, the post line to ~7,000 ft, the GPS station where it ends, and the unmarked ash slope above.
review.other_findings: None. Stored approach says 2.25 mi / 1,100 ft to timberline; sources say 2.1 mi to the Loowit junction at ~4,800 ft — consistent within rounding.
